question.title: Digital access to museum collections
question.text: Museums increasingly make their collections available online, but digital access is not simply a matter of uploading photographs. A useful digital record needs context. Visitors may need to know where an object was made, how it was used and why different communities value it. Accurate descriptions make collections searchable and help prevent misleading interpretations. Online access can benefit people who live far from a museum or cannot enter the building easily. It can also support teachers who want to compare objects from several institutions. Nevertheless, a photograph cannot reproduce every aspect of a physical object. Its scale, texture and surrounding exhibition may be difficult to convey. Digital projects also require continuing maintenance. Websites, file formats and accessibility requirements change, so institutions must budget for future updates. The strongest approach treats digital collections as a complement to physical visits, not a complete replacement. Technology is most useful when it broadens access while preserving the context that gives an object meaning.
facts: Digital museum records need reliable context, not photographs alone.
Descriptions explain origins, uses and significance and support searching.
Online collections improve access and help teaching.
Digital images cannot fully convey physical scale, texture or exhibition context.
Ongoing updates are needed, and digital access complements physical visits.
question.sample: The speaker argues that effective digital museum collections need accurate context as well as photographs. Descriptions help people understand an object’s origin and significance, while online access benefits distant visitors and teachers. However, images cannot fully reproduce physical qualities such as scale and texture. Digital collections also need continuing updates. They therefore work best as a complement to physical visits, broadening access without losing meaning.

question.title: Reducing food waste on campus
question.text: A university cafeteria that wants to reduce food waste should first find out where the waste occurs. Food discarded during preparation requires a different response from food left on customers’ plates. For example, better forecasting may prevent the kitchen from preparing too many portions, while allowing customers to choose a smaller serving may reduce plate waste. Staff should measure waste over several ordinary weeks rather than draw conclusions from one unusually busy day. The results can guide a small trial, such as changing portion sizes at one counter. Importantly, reducing waste does not mean ignoring food safety. Surplus food can only be redistributed when storage, handling and collection meet the relevant requirements. Communication also matters: customers may accept changes more readily if they understand the reasons and retain a choice of portions. Finally, the cafeteria should measure waste again after the trial. A successful programme uses evidence, tests practical changes and checks whether those changes actually produce a lasting improvement.
facts: Measure where and how much food is wasted before intervening.
Forecasting reduces overproduction; portion choices can reduce plate waste.
Collect representative data and trial a targeted change.
Redistribution must still satisfy food-safety requirements.
Explain changes and measure outcomes again to check lasting improvement.
question.sample: The lecture recommends an evidence-based approach to reducing cafeteria food waste. Staff should distinguish preparation waste from plate waste and collect data over several weeks. Better forecasting can reduce overproduction, while smaller serving options may help customers waste less. Any redistribution must remain safe. The speaker concludes that targeted trials, clear communication and follow-up measurements are needed to identify changes that work over time.

question.instruction: Listen to the three speakers once. Prepare for 10 seconds, then summarise their discussion within two minutes.
question.title: Extending library opening hours
turns: Maya

I think the library should stay open later throughout the semester, not only during exams. Some students work in the evening and need somewhere quiet afterwards. My shared house is noisy, so having access until midnight would make a real difference. What do you both think?
Ben

I understand the need, but opening the whole building could be expensive. We would need security, lighting and staff even if only a few students came. I would rather see a limited late-opening area, with student-card access, than promise a service the library cannot sustain.
Clara

A small area sounds sensible, but getting home safely is another issue. The last bus leaves before midnight. Students without cars might not benefit unless transport is considered too. Perhaps the university could coordinate a shuttle on the busiest nights rather than run it every evening.
Maya

That is a fair point. I do not need the borrowing desk to stay open; I mainly need a desk, power and internet. We could start with the ground-floor study room. A short survey might tell us which nights working students actually need it most.
Ben

I would support a trial based on that survey. We could count visits and check the cost for six weeks, then decide whether to continue. Clear rules would matter, especially about noise, visitors and what students should do if they need help after staff leave.
Clara

Then our recommendation could combine a small supervised study area with a transport check. We should ask students about both demand and travel, and make sure accessibility is included. That gives the university evidence before it commits to opening the entire library later.
facts: The discussion concerns later library access for students.
Maya supports later opening because work and noisy housing limit study opportunities.
Ben worries about cost and proposes a small card-access area with rules and a six-week trial.
Clara raises safe transport and accessibility, suggesting a shuttle on busy nights.
The group converges on surveying demand and trialling a limited study area alongside transport planning.
question.sample: The three students discuss extending library opening hours. Maya supports later access because students with jobs or noisy accommodation need a quiet place to study. Ben agrees there may be demand, but questions the cost of keeping the whole building open. He suggests a smaller area with controlled access, clear rules and a six-week trial. Clara adds that safe travel is equally important, since the last bus leaves before midnight, and proposes checking shuttle options and accessibility. Maya accepts the smaller-area idea because she mainly needs a desk and internet, not a borrowing service. The discussion therefore moves from a general request for longer hours towards a more practical proposal: survey students, trial a limited study space and consider transport before expanding the service.

question.title: Choosing a group-project format
turns: Daniel

For our environmental project, I would like to make a short video instead of a slide presentation. We could show the recycling facilities around campus and interview students. That might make our findings easier to understand than reading statistics from a screen during the final class.
Leah

A video could be engaging, but editing takes time and none of us has much experience. We also have to show how we collected and analysed our data. I worry that production work might distract us from the research, which is the main part of the assessment.
Omar

Could we combine the approaches? A few short clips could introduce the problem, followed by slides explaining the evidence. We should also provide captions and avoid filming anyone without permission. The format should help communicate the findings rather than become the main focus of the project.
Daniel

I like that compromise. We could record the facilities without identifying students, and use an anonymous questionnaire instead of interviews. I can take responsibility for two brief clips. If the clips do not work well, the research presentation would still be complete without them.
Leah

That makes the workload more manageable. Let us agree on the research questions and divide the analysis first. Then we can set a strict time limit for filming and editing. I would also like us to practise together so the final presentation feels like one coherent explanation.
Omar

Agreed. We should check the assessment instructions before committing, share a draft early and keep the clips short and accessible. The final plan is a slide-based presentation supported by video, with research quality, consent and clear teamwork taking priority over elaborate production.

question.title: 2014 Olympics
question.text:
11 February 2009 – Major athletic events around the globe – from the 2014 Sochi Olympics to an annual powerboat race in Norwegian fjords – are striving to neutralize their carbon footprint as part of a world-wide climate network, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) said today.

The sporting events are the latest participants to join the network, and are particularly important for inspiring further global action on the environment, said Achim Steiner, UNEP Executive Director.

"It is, therefore, heartening that this passion for excellence increasingly encompasses environmental performance, with sporting organizations raising the bar ever higher at each and every tournament," he added.

Organizers of the 2014 Sochi Olympic and Paralympic Winter Games – to be held in a unique natural setting between the shores of the Black Sea and the soaring snow-capped Caucasus Mountains – say they will put an estimated $1.75 billion into energy conservation and renewable energy.

That investment will be dedicated to improving transport infrastructure and offsetting greenhouse gas emissions from the use of electricity, air travel and ground transportation, the reforestation of Sochi National Park and the development of green belts in the city.

Africa is not homogeneous. The negative impression of Africa held internationally is very unfair to those African countries that are actually doing well in their development, because this continent has more than 50 countries rich in natural resources which have not been completely exploited and cultural diversity, and hardworking Africans are struggling to address issues of poverty, disease and war, so Africa can be an attractive place for business development and cultural tourism if concerted international support and assistance are provided. This skewed perception overlooks the vibrant reality and immense potential of the continent.

Africa has a lot of potential, and years ago it brought benefits to some companies. Historical engagements have proven that forward-thinking businesses can find success. In fact, Africa is the region with the best investment returns. It is a paradise for investors and adventurers, but it still needs international aid. It is good to do business with Africans because of the mutual money and long-term growth prospects. Furthermore, beyond business, Africa is also beautiful, boasting landscapes and cultural heritage that make it a premier destination for cultural tourism, offering profound experiences for visitors.

However, to discuss Africa honestly, one must also acknowledge its struggles. Africa suffers from frequent wars and the causes are complex, rooted in historical legacies and competition over resources, not in any inherent trait of its people. question.title: Television as a Relaxation Tool and Companion
question.text: Television serves many useful functions. It helps people to relax. Besides, it can also be seen as a companion for the lonely. To what extent do you agree with this? Explain why with your own experience.
keyPoints: Give a clear view about television as a relaxation tool and companion.
Explain how suitable programmes can reduce stress or provide entertainment.

Use relevant personal experience or an example to support the position.
question.sample:
Television can help people relax and can provide a sense of companionship, but I only partly agree that these are always useful functions. Its value depends on the programme, the amount of time spent watching and whether it supplements rather than replaces real relationships.

After a demanding day, a comedy, documentary or familiar series can give viewers a simple mental break. This kind of entertainment may reduce stress and help people shift their attention away from work or study. Television can also make a quiet home feel less empty. For example, an older person living alone may enjoy hearing presenters discuss everyday issues and may feel connected to a wider community.

However, television is not a true substitute for friendship. A viewer cannot receive personal advice, share responsibilities or develop mutual understanding with a programme. Excessive viewing may also reduce exercise, sleep and face-to-face conversation. Someone who watches television whenever they feel lonely might temporarily feel better while becoming even more isolated in the long term.

In my own experience, watching a short programme with my family helps us relax together because it creates a topic for conversation. By contrast, watching alone late at night often leaves me tired rather than refreshed. Therefore, television is a useful relaxation tool and limited companion, but people should combine it with active hobbies and genuine social contact.

question.title: Choosing bicycle parking
question.text: A college surveyed students before installing new bicycle parking. Many respondents wanted spaces near classroom entrances, but the design also needed to protect emergency access. Planners compared several locations and checked how bicycles would move through each area at busy times. They selected a site with clear visibility and enough room for people walking past. After installation, the college monitored use and invited feedback. This allowed minor problems to be corrected before the arrangement was expanded to other parts of the campus.

question.title: Recording local place names
question.text: Volunteers creating a local history map began by recording the place names used by older residents. Different names sometimes referred to the same location, so the team kept the original accounts and added explanatory notes. They did not assume that the most familiar spelling was always the oldest one. Instead, they compared memories with written records and identified uncertain details. The finished map showed both established information and questions that required further research, allowing readers to understand the evidence behind the labels.
